sources.title: Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters
sources.citation: NIST Special Publication 800-186, February 2023.
sources.notes: Primary standard read. Appendix C requires a large prime subgroup, small cofactor, non-anomalous order, and embedding degree at least 2^10 for recommended curves; Section 2 states the Hasse bound and subgroup definitions.

sources.title: Parallel Collision Search with Cryptanalytic Applications
sources.citation: Paul C. van Oorschot and Michael J. Wiener, Journal of Cryptology 12(1), 1999, pp. 1-28.
sources.notes: Publisher PDF read. Gives the random-mapping collision constant, distinguished-point method, useful-collision parameter q, and essentially linear wall-clock parallelism with a shared distinguished-point table.

sources.title: Using Symmetries in the Index Calculus for Elliptic Curves Discrete Logarithm
sources.citation: Jean-Charles Faugere, Pierrick Gaudry, Louise Huot, and Guenael Renault, Journal of Cryptology 27, 2014, pp. 595-635.
sources.notes: Publisher PDF read. Separates proven and heuristic PDP costs, states the factor-base pipeline and its two decomposition hypotheses, and explicitly warns that F4/F5 complexity has no general tight bound for irregular systems.

sources.title: A Taxonomy of Pairing-Friendly Elliptic Curves
sources.citation: David Freeman, Michael Scott, and Edlyn Teske, Journal of Cryptology 23, 2010, pp. 224-280.
sources.notes: Publisher PDF read. Defines embedding degree, explains target-field sizing, and records that supersingular curves have embedding degree 2 over prime fields and at most 6 in general.

sources.title: Quantum Resource Estimates for Computing Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithms
sources.citation: Martin Roetteler, Michael Naehrig, Krysta Svore, and Kristin Lauter, ASIACRYPT 2017; arXiv:1706.06752v3.
sources.notes: Author version read. Bounds one circuit family by 9n+2 ceil(log2 n)+10 logical qubits and 448 n^3 log2(n)+4090 n^3 Toffoli gates; these are logical circuit estimates, not physical-resource forecasts.

sources.title: Improved Quantum Circuits for Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithms
sources.citation: Thomas Haener, Samuel Jaques, Michael Naehrig, Martin Roetteler, and Mathias Soeken, PQCrypto 2020; arXiv:2001.09580.
sources.notes: Author version read. Improves reversible arithmetic and explores width/depth/T-count tradeoffs; explicitly treats resource estimates as circuit- and metric-dependent.

sources.title: Performance Analysis of a Repetition Cat Code Architecture: Computing 256-bit Elliptic Curve Logarithm in 9 Hours with 126133 Cat Qubits
sources.citation: Elie Gouzien, Diego Ruiz, Francois-Marie Le Regent, Jeremie Guillaud, and Nicolas Sangouard, Physical Review Letters 131, 040602 (2023); arXiv:2302.06639v2.
sources.notes: Author version read. The 9-hour/126133-cat-qubit estimate assumes a two- to one-photon loss ratio of 1e-5, 500 ns cycles, the paper's 2D architecture, routing, lattice surgery, and magic-state construction.

sources.title: Computing 256-bit Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithms in 26 Days on a Fault-Tolerant Trapped-Ion Quantum Computer with 20000 Qubits
sources.citation: Thomas Haener et al., arXiv:2609.05625v1, September 2026.
sources.notes: Preprint read, not treated as independently replicated. Reports about 1450 logical qubits and 40 million Toffoli gates, then an architecture-specific estimate of 19397 physical qubits, 25.7 days, and estimated 63% success for secp256k1.

sources.title: Concrete generic-interface audit
sources.citation: Method-by-method audit initiated in this corpus work.
sources.notes: The audit is an internal classification argument, not an external lower-bound theorem.

nodes.label: Hasse bound
nodes.statement: For an elliptic curve E over F_q, the group order satisfies |#E(F_q)-(q+1)| <= 2 sqrt(q).
nodes.scope: All elliptic curves over finite fields; the statement controls group size but not the factorization of the group order.
assumptions: E is an elliptic curve over F_q
nodes.quantifiers: For every finite field F_q and elliptic curve E/F_q.
non_implications: Does not imply that #E(F_q) is prime

nodes.label: Prime subgroup and cofactor
nodes.statement: Security is normally assigned to a prime-order subgroup <G> of order r inside E(F_q), with cofactor h=#E(F_q)/r.
nodes.scope: The full curve group may contain other components; protocols must specify subgroup membership or cofactor handling.

nodes.label: Quadratic-twist order relation
nodes.statement: For an elliptic curve E/F_q of trace t and its quadratic twist E', #E(F_q)=q+1-t and #E'(F_q)=q+1+t.
nodes.scope: Odd-characteristic statement in the standard quadratic-twist setting; analogous form-specific statements apply in characteristic two.
assumptions: E' is the quadratic twist of E

nodes.label: Embedding degree
nodes.statement: For a subgroup of prime order r with gcd(r,q)=1, the embedding degree k is the least positive integer satisfying r | (q^k-1).
nodes.scope: The degree relevant to MOV/Frey-Rueck transfer must be paired with the actual target-field representation and finite-field DLP cost.

nodes.label: Supersingular embedding-degree ceiling
nodes.statement: Supersingular elliptic curves have embedding degree 2 over prime fields of characteristic at least 5 and embedding degree at most 6 in general.
nodes.scope: With respect to relevant prime-order subgroups; exceptional small-characteristic details remain field- and subgroup-dependent.
assumptions: r is a prime subgroup order coprime to q
nodes.formula: k=2 over F_p (p>=5); k<=6 in general

nodes.label: Standard curve exclusion checklist
nodes.statement: A conventional curve-security screen requires a large prime subgroup, small cofactor, non-anomalous order, and sufficiently large embedding degree; it also records twist orders and validates public points.
nodes.scope: A parameter-screening condition, not a proof of ECDLP hardness. NIST SP 800-186 sets h<=2^10 and k>=2^10 for its generation criteria, while actual target-field security generally demands much more than merely meeting that floor.
assumptions: The point-count and subgroup-order computations are correct
The implementation enforces its validation rules
non_implications: Passing the checklist does not prove unrestricted classical ECDLP hardness

nodes.label: Concrete security experiment
nodes.statement: A concrete ECDLP claim fixes the instance distribution, success probability epsilon, preprocessing allowance, online time, memory, processor count, and cost unit.
nodes.scope: Asymptotic big-O notation alone does not determine a security level or comparable implementation cost.

nodes.label: Rho random-mapping heuristic
nodes.statement: If the iteration behaves as a random mapping on a state space of size N, the first repeated state occurs after about sqrt(pi N/2) steps in expectation.
nodes.scope: A birthday-model estimate. The useful ECDLP collision rate, partition function, fruitless cycles, and restart policy affect the real constant.
assumptions: A collision yields a nondegenerate linear equation with the accounted probability
nodes.quantifiers: Expectation over the modeled random mapping and random start.

nodes.label: Distinguished-point parallel collision search
nodes.statement: With m processors sharing distinguished endpoints, random-mapping collision search has leading wall time sqrt(pi N/(2u))/m iterations per processor for useful-collision probability u, plus distinguished-point tail and collision-location terms.
nodes.scope: The cited analysis is a random-function model with a central endpoint list. Total work remains birthday order; wall-clock speed is nearly linear only while communication, memory, and endpoint overhead remain controlled.
nodes.quantifiers: Expectation in the paper's random-mapping model.

nodes.label: Pollard lambda/kangaroo interval DLP
nodes.statement: When the logarithm is known to lie in an interval of width W, lambda/kangaroo methods solve it in expected O(sqrt(W)) group operations under their pseudorandom-walk heuristic.
nodes.scope: This is an interval problem, not full-width random ECDLP; constants and parallel variants depend on jump design.
assumptions: The jump walk mixes as modeled

nodes.label: Automorphism quotient speedup
nodes.statement: An efficiently computable automorphism action of effective orbit size a can reduce the collision space and suggests an approximately sqrt(a) rho speedup when the quotient walk remains random and orbit labels preserve the needed scalar relation.
nodes.scope: The effective orbit size may be smaller at stabilizers; negation and endomorphism folds can create fruitless cycles and do not automatically transfer to preprocessing lower bounds.

nodes.label: Negation-map fruitless-cycle obstruction
nodes.statement: Canonicalizing rho states under negation changes the walk and can introduce short fruitless cycles; a valid speedup requires an escape or cycle-handling rule and a costed implementation.
nodes.scope: Implementation-level qualification of the sqrt(2) quotient heuristic.

nodes.label: Cheon auxiliary-input attack
nodes.statement: If auxiliary powers such as [x^d]P are supplied and d divides r-1 in the specified strong-DH setting, the hidden exponent can be recovered faster than generic full-width DLP, with a tradeoff of the form O(sqrt(r/d)+sqrt(d)).
nodes.scope: Not an attack on a plain ECDLP instance (P,[x]P) without the required correlated auxiliary input; exact variants have different divisibility conditions.
assumptions: Required auxiliary group elements are available
non_implications: Does not lower the complexity of ordinary ECDLP without auxiliary powers

nodes.label: Frey-Rueck Tate-pairing transfer
nodes.statement: A nondegenerate Tate pairing can transfer an order-r elliptic-curve logarithm into the multiplicative group of an extension field containing the r-th roots of unity.
nodes.scope: Like MOV, usefulness depends on embedding degree, pairing nondegeneracy, extension representation, and the best finite-field DLP algorithm.
assumptions: Pairing is nondegenerate on the target subgroup

nodes.label: Target finite-field DLP governs pairing attack
nodes.statement: After a pairing transfer, the attack cost is the finite-field DLP cost in the minimal effective embedding field, not merely a function of k or q^k bit length in isolation.
nodes.scope: Field characteristic, extension structure, subgroup size, tower representation, and available NFS/small-characteristic algorithms all matter.

nodes.label: ECDLP index-calculus pipeline
nodes.statement: An ECDLP index-calculus attack selects an algebraic factor base, collects decompositions of random group combinations into base elements, solves the resulting sparse linear system for base logarithms, and performs an individual-log/descent step.
nodes.scope: All four stages and setup costs must be included. A decomposition oracle alone is not an end-to-end ECDLP algorithm.

nodes.label: Algebraic factor base
nodes.statement: A factor base F is a structured subset of curve points, normally chosen so membership/decomposition can be expressed by low-degree coordinate constraints; B=|F| determines both relation yield and linear-algebra dimension.
nodes.scope: A random list of B points and an algebraic set of B points have the same raw cardinality but potentially different recognition and solver costs.

nodes.label: Random decomposition-yield heuristic
nodes.statement: For m-sums drawn from a factor base of size B into a subgroup of size r, the mean ordered representation count over all targets is B^m/r; a random-target success probability is often approximated by 1-exp(-B^m/r), after symmetry and multiplicity conventions are fixed.
nodes.scope: The mean follows by counting, but Poisson behavior, variance, independence, field rationality, and solver visibility are heuristics. Unordered or signed conventions change constants.
assumptions: Tuple sums behave approximately independently for the Poisson approximation

nodes.label: Summation-polynomial degree growth
nodes.statement: For m>=3, the standard Semaev m-th summation polynomial is symmetric and has degree 2^(m-2) in each variable; its zeros encode x-coordinates of signed point tuples summing to the identity under the stated algebraic-closure conventions.
nodes.scope: Degree of the eliminated polynomial is not the same as the solving degree of a particular Weil-descended system.
assumptions: Characteristic and multiplicity conditions of the source
non_implications: Does not prove a low or high Groebner solving degree after Weil descent

nodes.label: Zero-dimensional PDP hypothesis
nodes.statement: Many summation-polynomial analyses assume the descended point-decomposition system is zero-dimensional, so it has finitely many algebraic-closure solutions and can be reduced to univariate solving.
nodes.scope: FGHR states this as Hypothesis 2; dimension can change on special targets, bases, or field equations.
assumptions: The chosen descended system is zero-dimensional

nodes.label: First-fall/regularity degree heuristic
nodes.statement: Binary and prime-field ECDLP estimates sometimes predict F4/F5 cost from a bounded first-fall, degree-of-regularity, or last-fall degree; equality between these quantities and the actual maximal solving degree is not automatic.
nodes.scope: A complexity exponent derived from this step remains conditional until the relevant degree is proved or measured on a scaling family without censoring failures.
assumptions: The selected degree predictor controls the actual solver trace
Coefficient specialization does not create harder components

nodes.label: Groebner cost depends on solving geometry
nodes.statement: F4/F5 cost is governed by Macaulay matrix sizes up to the maximal degree reached; for irregular affine systems there is no general tight bound, and change-of-order cost also depends on the quotient dimension D.
nodes.scope: This is a limitation on complexity inference, not a claim that every PDP instance is hard.
nodes.formula: FGLM=O(n D^3); F4/F5 matrix cost depends on d_reg/d_solve

nodes.label: Sparse relation-matrix solving
nodes.statement: Wiedemann/Lanczos-style sparse linear algebra solves the factor-base logarithm system using repeated sparse matrix-vector products; a B-column matrix with O(mB) nonzeros leads to a conventional O(m B^2) field-operation scale and O(mB) sparse storage, up to block and rank effects.
nodes.scope: The exact cost depends on coefficient field, block size, rank deficiency, relation filtering, and parallel architecture.
nodes.formula: T_LA roughly O(m B^2), storage O(mB)

nodes.label: Relation independence/rank heuristic
nodes.statement: Collecting roughly B plus a safety margin of relations is expected to span the B factor-base logarithms, but independence is a separate condition from relation count or decomposition success.
nodes.scope: Automorphism-folded columns, free relations, biased bases, and duplicate supports can change the rank profile.
assumptions: Relation rows behave sufficiently randomly over the scalar field

nodes.label: Gaudry fixed-extension index calculus
nodes.statement: For E/F_(q^n) with fixed n>=3, the Gaudry-style factor-base method with large-prime variants has a quoted soft-O(q^(2-2/n)) scale under its decomposition and polynomial-solving hypotheses, versus generic q^(n/2); constants grow exponentially with n.
nodes.scope: An asymptotic in q with n fixed. It does not imply a sub-rho algorithm for prime-field curves (n=1) or for cryptographic families where n grows without controlling the hidden dependence.
assumptions: Polynomial systems solvable at the assumed cost

nodes.label: Invariant-coordinate PDP speedup
nodes.statement: Permutation and curve-model symmetries can quotient PDP solution orbits and reduce change-of-order or matrix costs by exponential-in-m constants; FGHR separates a proven FGLM-side factor from a heuristic fast-change-of-order factor.
nodes.scope: A solver-stage speedup, not automatically an end-to-end exponent improvement; it requires the system and factor base to preserve the action.
assumptions: Regularity/randomization assumptions for heuristic change of ordering

nodes.label: Prime-field boundary for extension index calculus
nodes.statement: The q^(2-2/n) fixed-extension analysis obtains its advantage from n>=3; substituting n=1 is outside its setup and supplies no prime-field sub-rho conclusion.
nodes.scope: Does not exclude a different prime-field algebraic algorithm; it blocks one invalid extrapolation.
assumptions: The claimed attack is the Gaudry fixed-extension construction

nodes.label: PKM prime-field algebraic route
nodes.statement: Prime-field Kummer/PKM constructions encode factor-base membership and Semaev relations as structured polynomial systems; a sub-rho conclusion would require a scaling proof or validated bound for relation yield, solving degree, matrix size, rank, and end-to-end descent cost.
nodes.scope: Current repository measurements at small N are evidence about implementations and finite cells, not a theorem of bounded solving degree.
assumptions: Structured systems retain low solving complexity at cryptographic scale

nodes.label: Binary summation-polynomial Weil descent
nodes.statement: Over binary extension fields, Weil descent converts a summation-polynomial relation into a Boolean or multivariate system; predicted improvements depend on factor-base dimension and the actual solving/last-fall degree of the descended family.
nodes.scope: Distinct from GHS descent to a curve Jacobian. Published and internal degree claims must retain their first-fall/regularity assumptions.
assumptions: Descended systems have the predicted degree behavior
Relation probability and rank models hold

nodes.label: Xedni calculus lifting attack
nodes.statement: Xedni calculus lifts several random combinations of P and Q from E(F_p) to rational points on a curve over Q reducing to E, then seeks a Mordell-Weil linear dependence whose reduction reveals the discrete logarithm.
nodes.scope: Silverman's 'index backwards' construction is a characteristic-zero lifting/lattice route, not the Semaev/Gaudry factor-base index calculus pipeline.
assumptions: Suitable simultaneous lifts can be constructed
Lifted points become dependent with useful coefficients

nodes.label: Canonical-height obstruction to xedni
nodes.statement: JKSST's displayed C0/p success bound and linear waiting-time obstruction require a chain of height/discriminant, Lang, selected-lift, scalar-reduction, useful-relation, subgroup/cofactor, and repeated-trial hypotheses; under that complete chain classic xedni is asymptotically worse than square-root attacks.
nodes.scope: The external theorem is a strong conditional obstruction, not an unconditional refutation. A kernel-checked audit proves many finite components but leaves the algorithm-specific bridges explicit; the paper separately reports prohibitive practical lift odds.
assumptions: Selected lifts satisfy a family-uniform global-minimal-discriminant height comparison
Lang's canonical-height conjecture or a direct uniform height gap
Mordell-Weil packing hypotheses apply to the selected lifts
Good reduction and exact subgroup sampling correspondence
Every success selects a bounded relation with nonzero denominator
Uniform cofactor and Hasse conversion from subgroup order q to field prime p
A history-uniform conditional-hazard recurrence for adaptive trials
nodes.formula: one-shot Pr[success] <= C0/p (conditional); history-uniform hazard <= C0/p => E[T]=Omega(p)
nodes.quantifiers: For the classic xedni construction and fixed lifted-point count, after every stated bridge is instantiated uniformly as p grows.
non_implications: Does not prove an unrestricted classical lower bound for every lifting algorithm
A one-shot event bound alone does not prove an adaptive waiting-time lower bound
The scalar modulus is subgroup order q; replacing q by p needs an explicit bounded-cofactor bridge

nodes.label: Kernel-checked finite xedni core
nodes.statement: The Lean audit proves exact coefficient-box counts, a finite packing bound with visible fiber multiplicity, cyclic ECDLP extraction for a nonzero denominator, exact fixed-direction relation probabilities, Hasse/cofactor conversions from q to p, and a conditional finite-horizon hazard-to-Omega(p) waiting theorem.
nodes.scope: Kernel-checked finite and conditional components only. The audit deliberately does not assert that the xedni lift algorithm satisfies their bridge hypotheses.
assumptions: Each individual theorem's displayed finite hypotheses
Prime subgroup order q for the exact useful-event formula
History-uniform inverse-order hazard for the waiting theorem
nodes.formula: Pr[fixed useful relation]=(q-1)/q^2; uniform hazard O(1/p) => E[T]=Omega(p)
non_implications: Does not compose rational lifts with finite-field sampling
Does not establish the adaptive hazard premise for xedni

nodes.label: Xedni end-to-end bridge obligations
nodes.statement: An end-to-end xedni obstruction still needs a specified lift-selection algorithm, a selected-point height/minimal-discriminant theorem, Lang or a direct height gap, Mordell-Weil packing data, good-reduction and subgroup correspondence, useful-relation selection, a uniform cofactor bound, and an adaptive repeated-trial recurrence.
nodes.scope: These are the exact missing interfaces between the proved finite core and the conditional asymptotic conclusion; failure to close them is not evidence that xedni succeeds.

nodes.label: Exact codimension-three function-field lift density
nodes.statement: For the repository's frozen degree-6, monic-quadratic function-field xedni family, the exact lift probability is (1-2/p+p^-3)/(2p^3), so the limiting density exponent is 3 with leading constant 1/2.
nodes.scope: Exact only for the recorded family and count convention; it is a scoped obstruction, not a universal xedni theorem.
assumptions: Frozen polynomial family and slot distribution of EXP-XEDN-002
non_implications: Does not cover a different function-field lifting family

nodes.label: S3 rootfinding collapses to group subtraction
nodes.statement: For fixed curve points R and F, the roots in X of S3(x_R,x_F,X) are x(R-F) and x(R+F); an oracle that enumerates F and probes these roots in a base/pair table is a group-law table algorithm, despite its summation-polynomial description.
nodes.scope: Covers the repository's m=2 direct-subtraction and m=3 pair-table rootfinders. It does not classify higher-arity algebraic system solving.
assumptions: Nondegenerate affine additions or correctly handled exceptional cases
The membership structure is a stored point-key table

nodes.label: 2017 logical quantum circuit estimate
nodes.statement: One reversible-arithmetic construction solves ECDLP over an n-bit prime field using at most 9n+2 ceil(log2 n)+10 logical qubits and 448 n^3 log2(n)+4090 n^3 Toffoli gates.
nodes.scope: A 2017 logical-circuit upper estimate for a particular construction; it excludes surface-code layout, magic-state factories, physical error rates, routing, and later circuit improvements.
assumptions: Prime-field affine arithmetic construction in the paper
nodes.formula: Q<=9n+2 ceil(log2 n)+10; Toffoli<=448 n^3 log2(n)+4090 n^3
non_implications: Does not state the number of physical qubits or elapsed time on a specified architecture

nodes.label: 2020 reversible-circuit tradeoff frontier
nodes.statement: Windowing, pebbling, and a reformulated reversible binary-Euclidean inversion improve elliptic-curve point-addition circuits and produce distinct width, depth, and T-count optima rather than one scalar resource figure.
nodes.scope: Logical circuit construction and compiler estimates; physical-qubit and wall-time conversion remains architecture-specific.
assumptions: Affine Weierstrass arithmetic and Q# implementations in the paper

nodes.label: 2023 repetition-cat physical estimate
nodes.statement: Under a specified repetition-cat architecture, loss model, routing layout, and 500 ns cycle, the paper estimates a 256-bit elliptic-curve logarithm in 9 hours using 126133 cat qubits.
nodes.scope: Architecture scenario, not a lower bound or a hardware-independent forecast; assumes a single- to two-photon loss ratio of 1e-5 and the paper's error-correction and magic-state mechanisms.
nodes.formula: 126133 cat qubits; 9 h; mean 19 photons/cat under stated assumptions

nodes.label: 2026 trapped-ion secp256k1 preprint estimate
nodes.statement: A September 2026 preprint reports a secp256k1 logical circuit of about 1450 qubits and 40 million Toffoli gates, compiled to an estimated 19397 physical trapped-ion qubits, 25.7 days, and 63% success on its proposed architecture.
nodes.scope: Current preprint and architecture proposal, not peer-reviewed or independently replicated in this corpus; exact conclusions inherit its compilation, error, routing, and factory assumptions.
nodes.formula: ~1450 logical qubits; 40e6 Toffoli; 19397 physical qubits; 25.7 d; estimated success 63%

nodes.label: Gap Diffie-Hellman setting
nodes.statement: A gap-DH group is one where DDH is easy, often through a pairing or decision oracle, while CDH is still assumed hard.
nodes.scope: Demonstrates that DLP, CDH, and DDH assumptions cannot be substituted solely from their one-way reductions.

nodes.label: Schnorr-to-DL random-oracle reduction
nodes.statement: Forking-style proofs reduce Schnorr-signature forgery to discrete logarithm in the random-oracle model, with quantitative loss depending on query and success parameters.
nodes.scope: A protocol proof under a model and reduction loss, not an equivalence between real-world signature security and ECDLP cost.
assumptions: Reduction obtains two related accepting transcripts
non_implications: Does not make every elliptic-curve signature scheme exactly as hard as ECDLP

nodes.label: Invalid-curve and small-subgroup boundary
nodes.statement: If an implementation accepts points outside the intended prime subgroup, small-subgroup or twist points can leak scalar residues even when ECDLP in the intended subgroup remains hard.
nodes.scope: An implementation/protocol failure, not a faster algorithm for the specified ECDLP instance.
assumptions: Implementation omits required curve/subgroup validation or cofactor handling
non_implications: Does not contradict generic or unrestricted ECDLP hardness on valid inputs

nodes.label: Multi-target/nonuniform security conversion
nodes.statement: A single-target sqrt(r) estimate cannot be reused unchanged when an adversary receives many targets, amortizes curve-specific setup, or is granted free preprocessing; the exact advantage depends on the declared experiment and accounting.
nodes.scope: The CGK theorems cover precise generic advice/preprocessing models; concrete deployed multi-user systems require a matching reduction and target distribution.

nodes.label: End-to-end index-calculus exponent obligation
nodes.statement: No prime-field sub-rho claim is established until one parameter family simultaneously bounds factor-base generation, decomposition probability, polynomial solving, relation rank, sparse linear algebra, descent, memory, and verification in one cost model.
nodes.scope: Optimizing or proving one stage cannot be reported as the complete attack exponent unless the other stages are asymptotically no larger.

nodes.label: Protocol-to-problem assumption mapping
nodes.statement: Each deployed construction must be mapped to the assumption its proof actually uses—DLP, CDH, DDH, gap-DH, one-more variants, knowledge assumptions, or a random-oracle reduction—rather than being labeled generically 'ECDLP-based.'
nodes.scope: Corpus boundary for future protocol-specific expansion.

edges.statement: Hasse controls total group size; factorization and subgroup choice remain separate.
The ECDLP instance is posed in the declared prime-order subgroup, not an unspecified full curve group.
Pohlig-Hellman makes the largest prime divisor, hence the subgroup order r, the controlling generic security parameter.
The twist has a different known order whose small factors can become an attack surface if invalid points are accepted.
Invalid-curve leakage bypasses the intended problem rather than solving it.
The least k with r dividing q^k-1 determines the basic MOV target extension.
The Tate-pairing transfer uses an extension containing r-th roots of unity.
The small embedding degree explains the classical pairing vulnerability of supersingular curves used as ordinary ECC groups.
MOV replaces the elliptic-curve DLP by a finite-field DLP in the pairing target.
Frey-Rueck likewise reduces the problem to target-field DLP.
When the transfer hypotheses hold, target-field DLP cost upper-bounds ECDLP cost.
The named-curve conclusion is meaningful only after subgroup, anomalous, embedding, and validation checks.
The checklist rejects #E(F_q)=q.
The checklist imposes a large embedding-degree floor.
A named hardness assumption is incomplete without success and resource parameters.
Measured costs instantiate only their declared distributions, success criteria, and cost units.
The familiar square-root cost and leading birthday constant depend on the random-walk model.
Distinguished endpoints make many walkers contribute to one collision process.
Provides a parallel generic upper bound while preserving birthday-order total work.
Applies when auxiliary information restricts x to an interval of width W.
Orbit folding supplies the conventional square-root constant-factor estimate.
The quotient walk must explicitly handle short fruitless cycles.
A rho constant-factor heuristic does not itself prove a preprocessing lower bound with N replaced by orbit count.
Faster recovery applies only to the augmented instance with correlated auxiliary powers.
Protocol outputs must be checked for auxiliary-input structure before applying a plain-ECDLP estimate.
The pipeline specifies what must be costed for an index-calculus ECDLP claim.
The base determines relation vocabulary and matrix dimension.
Double counting proves the mean representation count; Poisson success and variance remain heuristic.
B and m set the raw tuple count B^m.
The recursive summation-polynomial construction yields exponential per-variable degree growth.
Summation polynomials form the core equations, but degree alone does not establish dimension.
Finite quotient dimension is needed for the conventional change-of-order stage.
A first fall is a predictor, not an automatic upper bound on maximal solver degree.
The missing scale law for solving degree prevents extrapolation of the finite PKM plateau.
Small binary degree cells do not bound cryptographic-scale matrices.
Sparse solving succeeds only after enough independent rows have been collected.
Sparse linear algebra is the factor-base logarithm stage.
Yield controls relation-collection and descent trial counts.
Gives a conditional faster upper bound on eligible fixed-degree extension-field families.
Zero-dimensional PDP systems are an explicit hypothesis in the quoted analysis.
Invariant coordinates reduce the PDP solver constant/exponent under the stated solver model.
The fixed-n extension analysis cannot be extrapolated to n=1.
Would be a prime-field coordinate attack if all scaling obligations are proved at sub-rho cost.
Published and experimental cost projections hinge on degree behavior.
Would improve binary ECDLP on families where the descended systems retain favorable degree and yield.
First/last-fall assumptions drive the claimed Boolean-system cost.
The current S3 rootfind-subtract and pair-table paths use only group operations, equality, public folding actions, and table membership after setup.
The collapse at arity 2/3 table enumeration says nothing about a genuine higher-arity algebraic solver.
Turns asymptotic quantum tractability into one explicit logical-circuit upper estimate.
Logical Toffoli/qubit counts still require physical error-correction and architecture translation.
Gap-DH retains CDH as the hard computational problem.
The setting explicitly makes the DDH decision easy.
Pairings can decide Diffie-Hellman tuples without necessarily solving CDH in the source group.
A successful forger is converted into a discrete-log solver under the proof's random-oracle and forking conditions.
Problem reductions do not identify which assumption a protocol theorem needs.
Each protocol and security notion needs its own model and quantitative reduction recorded.
CGK applies only after the deployed experiment is matched to its advice and online-query interface.
Security degrades according to target count and setup reuse, not a universal single-target rule.
PKM must close every pipeline stage in a shared asymptotic and concrete cost model.
The principal unrestricted escape route is a fully costed coordinate-aware prime-field algorithm.
Later circuits improve and trade width, depth, and T count, so the 2017 polynomial is not a permanent concrete frontier.
Provides improved logical circuit families for the group-arithmetic stage of Shor ECDLP.
Maps a logical ECDLP workload into one explicit physical cat-qubit scenario.
The physical estimate closes the mapping only for its declared architecture and noise assumptions.
Compiles a newer secp256k1 circuit into a proposed trapped-ion architecture.
The estimate is architecture-specific, preprint-stage, and not an implementation demonstration.
A useful Mordell-Weil dependence among valid lifts reduces to a scalar relation solving the finite-field instance.
Bounded dependence coefficients make a random reduced tuple useful with only order-1/p probability under the theorem's assumptions.
The conditional xedni repetition scale is linear in p, asymptotically worse than rho's square-root scale.
The frozen function-field variant has an exact p^-3 relation-source density, far below a square-root-competitive gate.
The internal exact density is an independent scoped negative and does not strengthen the external theorem outside its frozen family.

The kernel-checked finite counts, scalar extraction, exact event probabilities, q-to-p conversion, and conditional waiting theorem supply components of the JKSST chain without asserting its algorithm-specific bridges.
The displayed asymptotic obstruction becomes end-to-end only after the selected-lift, height, reduction, usefulness, cofactor, and adaptive-trial interfaces are composed.
The classic lift algorithm has not been shown to satisfy every premise needed by the finite core and conditional obstruction.
Kernel-checked endpoint theorems do not by themselves establish the missing correspondence with selected rational lifts and adaptive trials.

research_targets.label: End-to-end prime-field IC exponent ledger
research_targets.objective: Express every proposed prime-field index-calculus family as the maximum of setup, relation collection, algebraic solve, sparse linear algebra, descent, memory, and verification exponents under one parameterization.
research_targets.acceptance: For each family, a symbolic cost row states B(r), m(r), success probability, solver matrix dimensions, relation rank margin, memory, preprocessing reuse, descent, and the largest exponent; unknown cells remain explicit obligations.
research_targets.next_step: Populate PKM, FGHR-style symmetry, generic pair-table, and random-base controls from existing artifacts, refusing to rank rows with unmatched setup or censored solver failures.

research_targets.label: Multi-target and nonuniform ECDLP model
research_targets.objective: State concrete single-curve, many-target security experiments and connect them to CGK advice/preprocessing bounds without granting unpriced setup.
research_targets.acceptance: The model fixes target count and distribution, setup reuse, advice bits, preprocessing operations, online queries, memory, processor count, and success; every conversion is proved or labeled heuristic.
research_targets.next_step: Write the experiment and derive the best bound obtainable directly from CGK before importing any multi-user birthday heuristic.

research_targets.label: Named-curve pairing-transfer census
research_targets.objective: For each named curve, certify subgroup order, embedding degree, minimal effective target field, and current finite-field DLP estimate rather than using embedding degree alone.
research_targets.acceptance: Machine-checkable records include q, r, k, twist/tower representation, pairing nondegeneracy route, target subgroup size, finite-field algorithm family, and a reproducible cost citation.
research_targets.next_step: Start with repository named prime curves and the NIST SP 800-186 set; use exact modular-order certificates before estimating target-field DLP.

research_targets.label: Protocol assumption graph
research_targets.objective: Attach concrete protocols and proof models to DLP, CDH, DDH, gap-DH, one-more, and auxiliary-input assumptions with quantitative reduction losses.
research_targets.acceptance: Each protocol node names the security notion, adversary interface, proof model, source theorem, exact assumption, reduction direction, and loss; implementation validation requirements are separate edges.
research_targets.next_step: Add Schnorr/EdDSA, ECDH/HPKE, ECDSA, and pairing protocols as separate families after primary proof verification.

research_targets.label: Xedni bridge-composition audit
research_targets.objective: Turn the kernel-checked finite xedni core into either a fully scoped end-to-end conditional theorem for a specified lift family or a counterexample showing that one required bridge fails.
research_targets.acceptance: A machine-checked interface ledger instantiates lift selection, minimal-discriminant height comparison, Mordell-Weil packing, good reduction, subgroup sampling, nonzero-denominator selection, cofactor control, and adaptive conditional hazards; every unproved premise remains a named theorem hypothesis.
research_targets.next_step: Choose one explicit prime-field lift family and formalize the selected-lift-to-finite-subgroup correspondence before attempting the height or adaptive-hazard steps.
